'''Karl Hess''' (born 20 June 1945 in [[Trumau]], [[Austria]]) is the Swanlund Professor Emeritus in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] (UIUC).<ref name="Brownlee"/><ref name="ECE">{{cite web|title=Karl Hess Karl Hess Swanlund Professor Emeritus|url=https://ece.illinois.edu/directory/profile/k-hess|website=ECE Illinois|accessdate=19 October 2017}}</ref>
He helped to establish the [[Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology]] at UIUC.<ref name="Legacy">{{cite news|last1=McGaughey|first1=Steve|title=Hess leaves a huge legacy at Beckman, UIUC|url=https://beckman.illinois.edu/news/2006/04/042606|accessdate=20 October 2017|work=Beckman Institute|date=April 26, 2006}}</ref><ref name=Brown>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Theodore L.|title=Bridging divides : the origins of the Beckman Institute at Illinois|date=2009|publisher=University of Illinois|location=Urbana|isbn=978-0252034848|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ai13-61wGRoC&pg=PA7|accessdate=11 December 2014}}</ref>{{rp|7, 38}}

Hess is concerned with [[solid-state physics]] and the fundamentals of [[quantum mechanics]].  He is recognized as an expert in [[electron transport]], [[semiconductor physics]], [[supercomputing]], and [[nanostructures]].<ref name="McGaughey">{{cite news|last1=McGaughey|first1=Steve|title=Hess nominated for National Science Board|url=https://ece.illinois.edu/newsroom/article/253|accessdate=19 October 2017|work=ECE Illinois News|date=January 1, 2005}}</ref> 
A leader in  [[Simulation|simulating]] the nature and movement of [[electrons]] with [[Computer simulation|computer models]],<ref name="Brownlee">{{cite journal|last1=Brownlee|first1=Christen|title=Biography of Karl Hess|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=17 February 2004|volume=101|issue=7|pages=1797–1798|doi=10.1073/pnas.0400379101|pmid=14769927|bibcode=2004PNAS..101.1797B|pmc=383292|doi-access=free}}</ref>
Hess is considered a founder of computational electronics.<ref name="CAS"/>

Hess has been elected to many scientific associations, including both the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2001) and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (2003).<ref name="Brownlee"/> He has served on the  [[National Science Board]] (NSB).<ref name="McGaughey"/>

==Career==
Hess studied mathematics and physics at the [[University of Vienna]] in [[Vienna, Austria]], where he received his Ph.D. in 1970 in applied physics and mathematics.<ref name="Arakawa">{{cite book |last1=Arakawa |first1=Yasuhiko |title=Compound semiconductors 2001 : proceedings of the Twenty-eighth International Symposium on Compound Semiconductors held in Tokyo, Japan, 1–4 October 2001 |date=2002 |publisher=IoP Publ. |location=Bristol, U.K. |isbn=9780750308564 |page=vii |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s64c5E6IAPcC&pg=PR7 |accessdate=20 October 2017}}</ref><ref name="Legacy"/> 
He worked with Karlheinz Seeger on electron transport in semiconductors and subsequently became an assistant.<ref name="Seeger">{{cite journal |last1=Seeger |first1=Karlheinz |last2=Hess |first2=Karl F. |title=Momentum and energy relaxation of warm carriers in semiconductors |journal=Zeitschrift für Physik A |date=15 March 2005 |volume=237 |issue=3 |pages=252–262 |doi=10.1007/BF01398639 |bibcode=1970ZPhy..237..252S|s2cid=122290758 }}</ref>

In 1973 Hess went to the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) on a [[Fulbright scholarship]] to work with [[John Bardeen]]. With [[Chih-Tang Sah]] (the co-inventor of CMOS technology), Hess worked theoretically on electron transport in transistors, to find a solution of the [[Boltzmann equation|Boltzmann transport equation]] for transistors.<ref name="Brownlee"/><ref name="Legacy"/>

In 1974 Hess returned to the University of Vienna as assistant professor.  In 1977 he was offered a position as a visiting associate professor which enabled him to return to UIUC. Hess worked on improving the efficiency of [[charge-coupled devices]]. He and  [[Ben G. Streetman]] developed the concept of "real space transfer" to describe the performance of high-frequency transistors involving hot‐electron  [[thermionic emission]].<ref name="Brownlee"/><ref name="Streetman">{{cite journal |last1=Hess |first1=K. |last2=Morkoç |first2=H. |last3=Shichijo |first3=H. |last4=Streetman |first4=B. G. |title=Negative differential resistance through real-space electron transfer |journal=Applied Physics Letters |date=15 September 1979 |volume=35 |issue=6 |pages=469–471 |doi=10.1063/1.91172 |bibcode=1979ApPhL..35..469H}}</ref><ref name="Arakawa"/>
This work was important to the development of layered semiconductor technology.<ref name="Legacy"/>

In 1980 Hess was appointed to a full professorship for electrical engineering and computer science at UIUC.  He also undertook secret research at the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] from the 1980s onwards.<ref name="Brownlee"/>

Hess chaired one of two committees established in 1983 to consider the possible formation of a multidisciplinary research facility at the University of Illinois.<ref name="Bell"/><ref name=Brown/>{{rp|7}} In the fall of 1987, [[William T. Greenough]] and Karl Hess became associate directors of the [[Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology]] at UIUC.<ref name=Brown/>{{rp|xviii, 38, 92}} Hess later served as Co-chair of the Molecular and Electronic Nanostructures initiative at the Beckman Institute.<ref name="Bell">{{cite news |last1=Bell |first1=Trudy E. |title=The Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology 'Two heads are better than one' is an adage honored by this research institute, where multidisciplinary collaboration is an art |url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/the-beckman-institute-for-advanced-science-and-technology |access-date=20 October 2017 |work=IEEE Spectrum |date=1 Nov 1999}}</ref>

Hess became "a leading theoretician in the realm of semiconductor transistors".<ref name="Bell"/> His models of the behavior of transistors and integrated circuits enabled researchers to understand how they worked at fundamental levels and find ways to improve them.<ref name="Legacy"/>
His work on simulation of the behavior of electrons in semiconductors led to the [[Monte Carlo methods for electron transport|full-band Monte Carlo method]] of simulation.<ref name="Arakawa"/> This approach incorporated both the Boltzmann equation and aspects of quantum mechanics, using supercomputers to model electrons both as particles and as waves.<ref name="Brownlee"/>
He also developed simulations for the behavior of electrons in [[optoelectronics]], modeling [[Quantum well laser|quantum well laser diodes]], tiny lasers used in bar-code scanners, CD players, and fiber-optic technology.  Hess's algorithms were used for design software called MINILASE, enabling engineers to more quickly and accurately predict the effects of design modifications.<ref name="Brownlee"/><ref name="Arakawa"/>

From the 1990s onwards, Hess focused on nanotechnology and quantum informatics,<ref name="Brownlee"/>  including quantum transport in mesoscopic systems.<ref name="Leburton">{{cite book |last1=Hess |first1=K. |last2=Leburton |first2=J. P. |last3=Ravaioli |first3=U. |title=Computational Electronics Semiconductor Transport and Device Simulation |date=1991 |publisher=Springer US |location=Boston, MA |isbn=978-1-4757-2124-9}}</ref>
Around 1995, a conversation with nanolithographer Joseph W. Lyding suggested to Hess that using deuterium to passivate the surfaces of integrated circuits had the potential to increase the speed or the lifetime of the circuit. Hess and Isik Kizilyalli compared the degradation of CMOS transistor wafers prepared with either deuterium or hydrogen, and found that use of deuterium substantially increased transistor lifetimes.<ref name="Lyding">{{cite journal |last1=Hess |first1=K. |last2=Register |first2=L. F. |last3=Tuttle |first3=B. |last4=Lyding |first4=J. |last5=Kizilyalli |first5=I. C. |title=Impact of nanostructure research on conventional solid-state electronics: The giant isotope effect in hydrogen desorption and CMOS lifetime |journal=Physica E: Low-dimensional Systems and Nanostructures |date=October 1998 |volume=3 |issue=1–3 |pages=1–7 |doi=10.1016/S1386-9477(98)00211-2 |bibcode=1998PhyE....3....1H}}</ref><ref name="Kizilyalli">{{cite journal |last1=Kizilyalli |first1=I. C. |last2=Lyding |first2=J. W. |last3=Hess |first3=K. |title=Deuterium post-metal annealing of MOSFET's for improved hot carrier reliability |journal=IEEE Electron Device Letters |date=March 1997 |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=81–83 |doi=10.1109/55.556087 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3253329 |accessdate=23 October 2017 |bibcode=1997IEDL...18...81K|s2cid=13207342 }}</ref><ref name="Arakawa"/>
In 1996, Hess was named to the Swanlund Chair of Electrical and Computer and Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois.<ref name="DTIC1998"/>

Hess has written extensively about [[Hidden-variable theory|hidden variables]], a theoretical idea in quantum mechanics that has been hotly contested by many scientists since [[Albert Einstein]] and [[Niels Bohr]].<ref name="Legacy"/> 
Was quantum mechanics complete as a theory, or were not-yet-understood "hidden variables" required to explain phenomena such as "[[Action at a distance|spooky action at a distance]]"?<ref name="Economist">{{cite news |title=What is spooky action at a distance? |url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/economist-explains/2017/03/economist-explains-13 |accessdate=20 October 2017 |newspaper=The Economist |date=March 16, 2017}}</ref>  
In the 1960s, [[John Stewart Bell]] predicted that the question of hidden variables could be experimentally tested: the outcome of specific experiments based on the hypothetical [[EPR paradox|Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen]] (EPR) paradox should differ depending on whether or not hidden variables did or did not exist. 
Hess and mathematician Walter Philipp controversially claim that [[Bell's theorem]] is flawed. They argue that Bell's test can be made to fail by modeling temporal information. With this addition, existing experimental findings can be explained without resorting to hidden variables or "action at a distance".<ref name="Legacy"/><ref name="Philipp">{{cite journal |last1=Hess |first1=K. |last2=Philipp |first2=W. |title=Bell's theorem and the problem of decidability between the views of Einstein and Bohr |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=27 November 2001 |volume=98 |issue=25 |pages=14228–14233 |doi=10.1073/pnas.251525098 |pmid=11724942 |bibcode=2001PNAS...9814228H |pmc=64664|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Ball">{{cite journal |last1=Ball |first1=Philip |title=Exorcising Einstein's spooks Is there another layer of reality beyond quantum physics? |journal=Nature |date=29 November 2001 |doi=10.1038/news011129-15 |url=http://www.nature.com/news/2001/011129/full/news011129-15.html |accessdate=20 October 2017|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="loophole">{{cite journal |last1=Hess |first1=K. |last2=Philipp |first2=W. |title=A possible loophole in the theorem of Bell |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=27 November 2001 |volume=98 |issue=25 |pages=14224–14227 |doi=10.1073/pnas.251524998 |pmid=11724941 |pmc=64663 |bibcode=2001PNAS...9814224H|doi-access=free }}</ref>
Others have argued that Hess and Philipp's formulation does not depend on new time parameters, but rather on a violation of the assumption of [[Principle of locality|locality]] required by Bell.<ref name="Gill">{{cite journal |last1=Gill |first1=R. D. |last2=Weihs |first2=G. |last3=Zeilinger |first3=A. |last4=Zukowski |first4=M. |title=No time loophole in Bell's theorem: The Hess-Philipp model is nonlocal |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=31 October 2002 |volume=99 |issue=23 |pages=14632–14635 |doi=10.1073/pnas.182536499 |pmid=12411576 |pmc=137470 |arxiv=quant-ph/0208187 |bibcode=2002PNAS...9914632G|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Scheidl">{{cite journal |last1=Scheidl |first1=T. |last2=Ursin |first2=R. |last3=Kofler |first3=J. |last4=Ramelow |first4=S. |last5=Ma |first5=X.-S. |last6=Herbst |first6=T. |last7=Ratschbacher |first7=L. |last8=Fedrizzi |first8=A. |last9=Langford |first9=N. K. |last10=Jennewein |first10=T. |last11=Zeilinger |first11=A. |title=Violation of local realism with freedom of choice |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=1 November 2010 |volume=107 |issue=46 |pages=19708–19713 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1002780107 |pmid=21041665 |pmc=2993398 |bibcode=2010PNAS..10719708S|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Hess officially retired from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in May 2004, but remains the Swanlund Professor Emeritus.<ref name="McGaughey"/>
After his retirement,  Hess was nominated to the [[National Science Board]] (NSB) of the [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) by  President [[George W. Bush]], serving from 2006 to 2008.<ref name="McGaughey"/>
